pheidippides-announcing-the-victory-at-marathon

According to legend, a runner named Pheidippides raced from the battlefield of Marathon to Athens to announce that the Greeks had beaten the Persians, then collapsed and died. Luc-Olivier Merson painted the moment he reaches the city in 1869, and the legend is why a long-distance race is called a marathon.
the-battle-of-salamis

Wilhelm von Kaulbach shows the sea battle of 480 BC in which the Greek ships crushed the Persian fleet of King Xerxes in the narrow waters near Athens. It is a giant painting full of tangled ships, flying spears and a sky glowing over the water, made to celebrate the victory that kept Greece free.
phidias-showing-the-frieze-of-the-parthenon-to-his-frie

The sculptor Phidias shows Pericles and a circle of Athenian friends the carved marble frieze made for the Parthenon, the great temple on the Acropolis. Lawrence Alma-Tadema, famous for his research, painted this Athens of the 400 BC golden age in 1868, long before the real frieze was properly understood.
the-school-of-athens

Raphael filled a Vatican room with the great thinkers of ancient Greece: Plato points up at the sky of ideas while Aristotle holds out a hand toward the Earth. Painted around 1511 at the height of the Italian Renaissance, it says that the new age was a rebirth of the clear thinking of ancient Athens.
alcibiades-receiving-a-lesson-from-socrates

The philosopher Socrates teaches the young Alcibiades, a brilliant and very spoiled Athenian aristocrat who later became a famous general and then a traitor. François-André Vincent painted it in 1776, when French artists were turning to stories of ancient Greece and Rome.
socrates-and-alcibiades

Christoffer Wilhelm Eckersberg paints the wise old Socrates and the handsome young Alcibiades in the Athens of the 400s BC. The Danish painter made this in the 1810s, when artists were studying ancient Greece closely for new ideas.
the-symposium-after-plato

Guests recline at a dinner party in ancient Athens, taking turns to give speeches about love, in a scene from Plato's dialogue The Symposium. Anselm Feuerbach, who loved ancient Greece, made two versions of it and painted this second one in the early 1870s.
plague-in-an-ancient-city

A terrible illness has struck an ancient city and people are dying in the streets. Michiel Sweerts painted it around 1652 and it is often connected to the plague that hit Athens in 430 BC during the long war with Sparta, an event that shook the golden age.
aristotle-with-a-bust-of-homer

The philosopher Aristotle, dressed in rich 1600s clothes, rests a hand on a bust of the poet Homer and seems lost in thought about wisdom, fame and money. Rembrandt painted it in 1653, and it is one of the most famous pictures of a thinker in all of art.
the-funeral-of-miltiades

Miltiades, the Athenian general who won at Marathon, died in disgrace, and his son Cimon agreed to take his place in prison so that his father could have a proper funeral. Jean-François Pierre Peyron painted this story of loyalty in 1782 for the Paris Salon.
the-battle-of-alexander-at-issus

Thousands of tiny soldiers swarm across a landscape of mountains, sea and glowing sky in Albrecht Altdorfer's view of Alexander the Great beating the Persian king Darius at Issus in 333 BC. He painted it in 1529 for a duke of Bavaria and made it feel like a whole world, not just a battle.
the-entry-of-alexander-into-babylon

Alexander rides into Babylon on a chariot in 331 BC with elephants, flower petals and cheering crowds. Charles Le Brun painted this for King Louis XIV of France, who loved being compared to Alexander.
the-passage-of-the-granicus

Alexander's cavalry charges across the Granicus river in 334 BC, the first big battle against the Persians. It is the first of five huge paintings Charles Le Brun made for Louis XIV about Alexander's victories.
alexander-and-porus

The Indian king Porus, who fought bravely and lost, is brought before Alexander. Alexander asks how he wants to be treated and Porus answers, like a king, and Alexander lets him keep his kingdom. Charles Le Brun painted the scene in 1673.
the-family-of-darius-before-alexander

After the Battle of Issus, the mother and family of the defeated Persian king kneel before Alexander. The queen mother bows to Alexander's friend Hephaestion by mistake, and Alexander kindly says he is Alexander too. Paolo Veronese painted this story of mercy around 1570.
the-battle-of-alexander-against-darius

Pietro da Cortona paints a whirlwind of horses and spears as Alexander charges at the Persian king Darius. Painted in the 1600s for a Roman family, it treats an ancient victory as an energetic Baroque spectacle.
the-battle-of-gaugamela

Jan Brueghel the Elder spreads thousands of tiny soldiers across a sunlit plain for the battle that ended the Persian Empire, probably Alexander's win over King Darius. Painted in 1602, it is full of little details to hunt for.
alexander-and-diogenes

Alexander the Great, who has everything, offers the philosopher Diogenes anything he wants. Diogenes, lying in the sun, just asks him to stop blocking the light. Gaspar de Crayer painted this meeting in the 1620s.
alexander-cuts-the-gordian-knot
According to legend, whoever could untie the huge Gordian knot would rule Asia. Alexander drew his sword and cut straight through it. Jean-Simon Berthélemy painted this clever solution in 1767.
alexander-the-great-and-roxane
Alexander the Great sits with Roxane, the Bactrian princess he married in 327 BC. Pietro Rotari painted this gentle scene in 1756 as a romantic story from the life of the famous conqueror.
romulus-and-remus

According to Roman legend, the twin babies Romulus and Remus were left by a river and fed by a she-wolf until a shepherd found them. Peter Paul Rubens painted this origin story of Rome around 1615, with the river god Tiber looking on.
cloelia-crossing-the-tiber

A young Roman woman named Cloelia, held hostage by the Etruscan king Porsena, escapes and leads other hostages across the Tiber river. Peter Paul Rubens painted the daring escape with his usual energy and glowing skin tones.
horatius-cocles-defending-the-bridge
The legendary Roman soldier Horatius Cocles holds a bridge alone against an enemy army while his friends chop it down behind him. Charles Le Brun painted the story of early Roman courage around 1642.
cincinnatus-leaves-the-plow-to-dictate-laws-to-rome

The Roman farmer Cincinnatus is called from his field in 458 BC and made dictator to save the city, then gives up power after only a few days and goes back to his farm. People later compared George Washington to him. Juan Antonio de Ribera painted it around 1806.
coriolanus-at-the-gates-of-rome

The Roman general Coriolanus, exiled by his own city, marches on Rome with an enemy army, but his mother and wife beg him to stop and he turns back. Franz Anton Maulbertsch painted this moving scene in the 1790s.
the-shepherd-faustulus-bringing-romulus-and-remus-to-hi

The shepherd Faustulus brings the two baby twins, found beside the wolf, home to his wife to raise. In Roman legend they grew up to found the city of Rome. Nicolas Mignard painted this tender scene in 1654.
romulus-and-remus-sheltered-by-faustulus
A shepherd family takes in the twin babies who will one day found Rome, in a calm, sunlit scene full of warm colors. Pietro da Cortona painted it in 1643.
lucretia

Lucretia, a noble Roman woman, stands with a dagger after a terrible wrong, and according to legend her death made the Romans drive out their last king in 509 BC and create the Republic. Rembrandt painted her thoughtful face in 1664, near the end of his life.
the-rape-of-the-sabine-women

In Roman legend the young city of Rome had no wives, so Romulus's men carried off the women of the neighboring Sabine tribe. Nicolas Poussin painted this chaotic scene in 1634 in his calm, classical style.
the-oath-of-hannibal

The boy Hannibal swears at an altar to hate Rome forever, with his father Hamilcar watching. Benjamin West painted it in 1770 while visiting Rome as a young American artist, and later George III bought it.
the-death-of-paulus-aemilius-at-the-battle-of-cannae

At the Battle of Cannae in 216 BC, Hannibal's army surrounded and crushed a larger Roman army, one of the greatest defeats in Roman history. John Trumbull painted this scene of the dying Roman consul Paulus Aemilius in 1773 as an early work.
the-continence-of-scipio
The Roman general Scipio Africanus returns a captured young bride to her fiancé instead of keeping her as a prize, a famous story about self-control. Nicolas-Guy Brenet painted it in 1788.
the-continence-of-scipio-nicolas-poussi
The same story of fairness in war: Scipio hands a captive woman back to her fiancé. Nicolas Poussin painted it around 1640 with the careful, classical order that he was known for.
the-clemency-of-scipio
Giovanni Bellini painted this long, stone-colored picture around 1506 to look like an ancient Roman carved frieze, telling a story of Scipio's mercy.
hannibal-s-crossing-of-the-alps
Hannibal's elephants and soldiers struggle over a steep snowy pass in the Alps in 218 BC on their way to attack Rome. Heinrich Leutemann made this dramatic picture in 1866.
the-battle-of-zama

A long Renaissance chest-panel shows the Battle of Zama in 202 BC, where Scipio finally beat Hannibal and ended the Second Punic War. The artist is known only as the Master of the Battle of Anghiari, and the painting was made around 1470.
the-battle-of-zama-cornelis-cort
A crowded engraving of the Battle of Zama, where Scipio defeated Hannibal in 202 BC. Cornelis Cort made it in 1567 from a Renaissance design, and prints like this spread famous stories across Europe.
the-murder-of-caesar

On the Ides of March in 44 BC, Roman senators, including Caesar's friend Brutus, stabbed Julius Caesar in the Senate. Karl von Piloty painted the moment just after in 1865 with Caesar lying beneath his statue.
cicero-denounces-catiline-in-the-roman-senate

In 63 BC the great speaker Cicero stands and accuses Catiline of plotting against Rome, and the other senators move away from him. Cesare Maccari painted this fresco in the 1880s for the Italian Senate.
vercingetorix-throws-down-his-arms-at-the-feet-of-juliu

The Gaulish chief Vercingetorix surrenders to Julius Caesar in 52 BC after the siege of Alesia, ending a big revolt against Rome. Lionel Royer painted it in 1899, when French people thought of Vercingetorix as their first national hero.
marius-at-minturnae

The Roman general Marius, hiding from enemies in a marsh, stares down the soldier sent to kill him, who drops his sword. Jean Germain Drouais painted this tense moment from the civil wars before Caesar in 1786.
caius-marius-amid-the-ruins-of-carthage
The exiled Roman general Marius sits alone among the ruins of Carthage, a symbol of how quickly fortune changes. John Vanderlyn painted it in Paris in 1807, and it won a gold medal from Napoleon.
